title: Futures vs Stocks
hook: A futures chart might look like every other chart. What you're trading underneath it isn't the same.

launchpad.outcome: Name the structural differences between trading futures and trading stocks — not just "futures move faster."
launchpad.missionQuestion: Can you treat 10 shares of a stock and 10 futures contracts as the same size?

markers.label: Stocks vs. futures side by side

beats.heading: Contract month, expiration, rollover, margin
beats.body: You'll hear these terms a lot. For now: futures contracts have a defined contract month and expiration, can require a rollover into the next contract, and use a margin structure different from a typical stock account. You don't need to master all of it today.

right.label: Futures
points: Nearly 24-hour weekday trading for many contracts

blocks.heading: What's wrong with Maya's reasoning?
blocks.scenario: Maya normally trades 10 shares of a stock. She decides she'll trade 10 MNQ contracts because "10 is my normal size."

options.label: Share quantity and futures contract quantity aren't economically equivalent units of risk
options.feedback: Right — 10 shares and 10 contracts can carry wildly different dollar risk. The number alone means nothing without knowing what a unit is worth.

options.label: Nothing — 10 is 10, no matter what she's trading
options.feedback: The unit matters. 10 shares of a stock and 10 futures contracts are not comparable sizes.

blocks.quote: Position size only means something when you understand what one unit of your instrument is worth.

seeIt.heading: Stocks ≠ Futures
seeIt.prompt: Same-looking charts. Watch the structures build up side by side.

stages.caption: Stocks: you're trading shares — equity ownership. No contract expiration. Trading hours: regular session, plus some extended hours.
Futures: you're trading standardized contracts — no ownership stake. Contracts expire, so rollover applies. Nearly 24-hour weekday trading for many contracts.
The terms you'll hear: contract month, expiration, rollover, margin. Futures use a margin structure different from a typical stock account — you don't need to master all of it today.
What actually matters: position size only means something when you understand what one unit of your instrument is worth — and stocks and futures are not the same unit.

rounds.question: A trader wants to profit from a short-term price move without caring about long-term company ownership. Which instrument type is built for that, and why?

options.label: Futures — a futures contract is based purely on price movement, not ownership
options.why: Futures contracts are built purely around price movement, with no ownership stake.

options.label: Stocks — stock ownership was always designed for short-term moves
options.feedback: Stock ownership is fundamentally about owning a piece of a company, not short-term price speculation.

options.label: Neither — instrument choice has nothing to do with that goal
options.feedback: Instrument choice matters a lot here — futures are specifically built around price movement.

rounds.question: What's the core difference between what you own when you buy a stock versus what you hold in a futures contract?

options.label: A stock is a claim on company ownership; a futures contract is an agreement based on price movement
options.why: Buying a stock means owning a piece of a company. A futures contract carries no ownership stake at all.

options.label: They're the same thing with different names
options.feedback: They're structurally different — one is ownership, one isn't.

options.label: A futures contract is a type of stock
options.feedback: A futures contract isn't a stock at all — no ownership stake.

sayItBack.prompt: Imagine another AGHF girl asks: "Why can't I just trade the same number of contracts as shares I used to trade?" How would you explain it to her?
sayItBack.modelAnswer: Because a share and a contract aren't the same unit of risk. One share of a stock might be worth $50, while one futures contract's point value could be worth $2, $5, or $50 per point depending on the instrument. The number 10 doesn't mean anything on its own — you have to know what one unit of whatever you're trading is actually worth before size means anything.

checklist: Stocks are ownership; futures are standardized contracts on price movement.
Futures contracts expire and involve rollover — stocks don't.
Share count and contract count are not equivalent units of risk.
Know what one unit of your instrument is actually worth.

takeaways: Stocks are ownership; futures are standardized contracts on price movement.
Futures contracts expire and involve rollover — stocks don't.
Share count and contract count are not equivalent units of risk.
remember: Know what one unit of your instrument is actually worth.
